title: American YouTuber Ed Nathanson Says Indian Food Has 'Literally Ruined' All Other Cuisines for Him
excerpt: The self-proclaimed 'World's Greatest Snack Detective' says discovering pani puri, chicken vindaloo, and gobi Manchurian five years ago permanently changed his palate — and his viral video has Indian food lovers inviting him to visit India.
body:
• US-based content creator Ed Nathanson shared an Instagram video declaring Indian food has "literally ruined all other cuisines" for him since he discovered it five years ago
  • His favorites include pani puri, chicken vindaloo, and gobi Manchurian — and he says Indian cuisine even converted him from a "hardcore carnivore" to someone who willingly orders vegetarian dishes
  • The video went viral, with viewers urging Nathanson to visit India and try the food in its home country
  • His enthusiasm reflects a broader global trend: Indian cuisine is now a $15 billion market in the US alone, with regional dishes moving from niche to mainstream

A 'Problem' With Indian Food

Ed Nathanson has a problem with Indian food. His problem is that he likes it far too much.

Nathanson, a US-based content creator who calls himself the "World's Greatest Snack Detective," shared a video on Instagram explaining how discovering Indian cuisine roughly five years ago fundamentally changed the way he thinks about food.

"I have a problem with Indian food. It has literally ruined all other cuisines for me."

— Ed Nathanson, content creator

"It's like the heavens opened," Nathanson said, describing the moment Indian food first entered his life. Since then, he has assembled a list of favorites that reads like a tour through India's street food stalls and restaurant kitchens.

Pani puri tops his list — he called the crispy shells filled with spiced water "little flavour bombs that explode in your mouth." Chicken vindaloo earned the description "lightning strike of deliciousness." Gobi Manchurian also made the cut, according to a report by NewsPoint.

A Carnivore Converted

What stands out about Nathanson's experience is not just his enthusiasm but how thoroughly Indian cuisine reshaped his eating habits. He described himself as a former "hardcore carnivore" who now willingly orders vegetarian dishes because Indian cooking makes vegetables genuinely exciting.

"My palate is literally changed forever," he said.

Nathanson reserved his sharpest humor for comparing Indian food to Western cuisine. "Now you expect me to get excited because you put a little rosemary on your chicken breast?" he joked, contrasting the dozens of spices in a single Indian dish with the restrained seasoning common in many American kitchens. When he brought up garlic aioli as a supposed flavor innovation, his response was blunt: "Oh, does it, Linda?"

His verdict for other cuisines was two words: "Do better." For Indian food: "Keep doing your delicious you."

Viewers Want Him in India

The video quickly went viral, drawing thousands of comments from Indian food lovers who pointed out that Nathanson has only scratched the surface. Many urged him to visit India, arguing that the American versions of dishes like pani puri barely hint at what the originals taste like.

"Once you go brown, the other colours let you down," one commenter joked, according to NewsPoint. Another suggested that if American pani puri had already won him over, trying it in India might convince him to become a permanent resident.

This is not Nathanson's first time championing Indian cuisine online. When TasteAtlas ranked India 12th on its list of the world's best cuisines, the creator went on a viral rant calling the ranking "culinary disrespect," according to CurlyTales. "You're telling me that the country that gave us biryani, butter chicken, samosa, vada pav, pani puri, dosa, and 600 kinds of chutneys is not in the top 10?" he said.

Part of a Bigger Wave

Nathanson is not alone in his conversion. As Pravasi Samwad reported, international food vloggers and influencers have increasingly been documenting their experiences with regional Indian dishes, introducing audiences outside India to foods well beyond the familiar curry and naan. Another American creator, Drew Hicks, who speaks Hindi, has similarly attracted attention for his love of Indian food and his humorous reactions to the high price of samosas in the US.

The trend tracks with hard numbers. Indian cuisine represents a $15 billion market in the US, with over 40,000 Indian restaurants nationwide, according to industry data. The number of high-end Indian restaurants in the country rose from 101 in 2018 to 154 in 2025. Datassential, an F&B intelligence platform, identified regional Indian cuisine — particularly Keralan food — as one of the fastest-rising culinary trends for 2026, with 39 percent of US consumers expressing interest in trying it.

Gen Z Americans are driving much of the curiosity, exploring dishes like biryani, chaat, dosa, and South Indian formats that go far beyond the tikka masala and butter chicken that once defined Indian food in the American imagination.

What's Next

For the Indian diaspora in the US, viral moments like Nathanson's carry weight beyond entertainment. Each one nudges Indian food further into the American mainstream, potentially boosting foot traffic at local Indian restaurants and normalizing a cuisine that many first-generation immigrants grew up being teased about bringing to school.

As for Nathanson, someone still needs to get this man to India.
